items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] Al Rose was telling me that... [INTERVIEWEE] Yeah, occasionally some of the other musicians do it today...

ctx.x: Yeah, the Ori band always used it. Of course, Bud Scott, in the days I heard him, he always played guitar, too. He could play banjo, might have done it on a few special numbers sometime, but almost always just guitar. And the Ori band also softened down a lot at times. I mean, they had a lot of variety and dynamics, you might say. But that was part of the old New Orleans tradition, and Jelly talks about it, but Jelly also talks about they would be probably New Orleans bands, too. He was objecting to, being loud.…

Al Rose was telling me that when he grew up listening in the bands that the clarinet and the trumpet always were in harmony together, and the clarinet was not a counterpoint to the trumpet, but he rarely hears that now, that Harry Shields was the last one he knew of that actually harmonized with the trumpet player.

Yeah, occasionally some of the other musicians do it today, but to me, I never heard music here before, say 1930, 38 maybe, it was the first time I ever heard any music here. And so all we have to do, go by, are the old records. But to me, that's been more, to me, a more later development. Some people try to make a big difference between the terms like Dixieland and traditional New Orleans jazz and all, which is mainly just words in people's minds. Because like Bunk once said, we always called it ragtime, and…

items.q: as Al Rose was saying the last time I saw him

ctx.x: me but my left hand Jelly said this but my left hand enabled me to beat Tony so he thought he knew he had a little something probably that Tony Jackson didn't have too as Al Rose was saying the last time I saw him Al spent a lot of money recording a whole album of Tony Jackson music having Naki Parker play it hoping that he could recapture some of the style not knowing how Tony played either nobody does hardly now but it looks like Tony most of those pieces were not so hot so maybe Tony wasn't quite as great as…
he was a good piano player but he wasn't much of a composer

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: Al Rose, whom you met and has been very helpful at times in our project, was traveling around making his cartoons in colleges and was in Texas and said he'd try to find him. I gave him all the dope I had.

ctx.x: Well, maybe you could correct him.

A footnote or something like that. Yes, sort of evaluate some of that, too. I'd rather do that and not take a lot of time on the tape now to do that. And they're not in a condition to be photostadded or Xerox or whatever it is. Another man who's dead now, Buddy Christian, an outstanding banjo and guitar player from New Orleans, who also played piano here and also in New York. And he played on quite a few of the Clarence Williams Hot Five. And what are they called? Blue Five, excuse me. Anyway, he's been dead for…
